1296.title: Laodicea (Revelation 3:14–22)
1296.hook: lukewarm; and yet: behold, I stand at the door and knock
1296.howItsDone: Revelation 3:20 is used in some churches as an invitation to welcome Christ personally, and appears in hymns, sermons and paintings of Christ knocking at a door.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Philadelphia: a little strength, and a door no one can shut. Your line was an open door.

A bath, run and then forgotten for an hour. You step in and flinch. Not hot enough to comfort, not cold enough to refresh. Just lukewarm. The seventh letter in Revelation, to the church of the Laodiceans, reaches for exactly that picture, and doesn't soften it. But stay to the end. Right after the hard words comes a quiet picture: someone standing outside a door, knocking, waiting to be let in for supper.

First, the verdict: "I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot. So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth." Readers hear this two ways. Some take hot and cold as passion and refusal: a complaint about half-heartedness. Others hear water: hot water that heals, cold water that refreshes, lukewarm water good for neither; some link it to the water supply around the city. Second, how the church saw itself: "I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing." How the letter sees it: "wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked." So the counsel: buy gold tried in the fire, white clothes to cover them, and salve for their eyes, "that thou mayest see." Third, why say any of this: "As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent." The hard words come from love, the letter says, not from contempt. Fourth, the knock: "Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me." Sup means share supper. Notice where the speaker stands: outside a door, asking to come in. Some preachers use this verse to invite one person to open their life to Christ. Others stress that it's spoken first to a whole church. The words say "any man": the door opens one person at a time, and on the other side is a meal.
screen: `I AM RICH, AND HAVE NEED OF NOTHING.`
`AS MANY AS I LOVE, I REBUKE.`
`I STAND AT THE DOOR, AND KNOCK.`

segments.voice: Picture a door, and someone on the other side knocking gently, not hammering, waiting. If you pray, say the verse slowly, "Behold, I stand at the door, and knock," then listen, and if you choose, open it; if you don't pray, let it be a door you've kept shut on someone, a call not returned, a friend held at arm's length, and picture your hand on the handle. You don't have to decide anything yet; just notice the knock.
Laodicea. The lukewarm church that thought it needed nothing, rebuked out of love, with Christ outside its door, knocking.
Your line: I stand at the door. Hard words, and then an offer of supper. See you tomorrow.

1297.title: The throne room (Revelation 4)
1297.hook: a rainbow, a sea of glass, creatures crying holy
1297.howItsDone: In the communion services of some churches, the congregation sings or says the 'Holy, holy, holy' (the Sanctus), joining the song of Isaiah 6 and Revelation 4, and the hymn 'Holy, Holy, Holy! Lord God Almighty' draws on this chapter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Laodicea: lukewarm, and yet someone standing at the door, knocking. Your line was I stand at the door.

Yesterday's letter ended with Christ outside a door, knocking. Today the door swings the other way. "After this I looked, and, behold, a door was opened in heaven." A voice like a trumpet says, "Come up hither." The letters to the seven churches are done. John, the exile on Patmos, is invited up through the door, into the room the rest of the book keeps coming back to: the throne room. Today, a look through the doorway with him.
screen: `THE ROOM THE BOOK KEEPS COMING BACK TO.`

segments.voice: First, the throne. John describes no face, only light and stone: "he that sat was to look upon like a jasper and a sardine stone: and there was a rainbow round about the throne, in sight like unto an emerald." Some readers hear in that rainbow the bow God set in the clouds after the flood, a sign of promise. John doesn't say; he just reports the green light circling the throne. Second, around it: twenty-four elders in white with crowns of gold, lightning and thunder, and "before the throne there was a sea of glass like unto crystal." The text doesn't explain the sea; it lets you stand at the edge of it. Third, the creatures. The King James calls them beasts; the sense is living creatures. One like a lion, one like a calf, one with the face of a man, one like a flying eagle. Full of eyes, with six wings, and "they rest not day and night, saying, Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, which was, and is, and is to come." It echoes Isaiah, who heard seraphim cry, "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts." A later Christian tradition matched the four faces to the four Gospel writers, and you may still see a lion, an ox and an eagle carved on a pulpit. Fourth, the elders. Every time the creatures sing, they fall down and "cast their crowns before the throne." Whatever honor they were given, they lay it down. In some churches' communion services, the congregation joins that same song: holy, holy, holy.

Close your eyes if that's comfortable, and let a rainbow appear, green as an emerald, curved around a light you don't try to look into, a sea of glass perfectly still at your feet, and somewhere a soft, steady sound that never stops. If you pray, join the creatures' words, one on each breath: holy, holy, holy; if not, stay at the edge of the glass and let the stillness hold you.
The throne room. John's vision through an open door in heaven: a rainbow like emerald, a sea of glass, and creatures who never stop saying holy.
Your line: holy, holy, holy. Sung day and night in that room. That's today, done.

1298.title: The slain Lamb (Revelation 5)
1298.hook: the lion of Judah turns out to be a Lamb that was slain
1298.howItsDone: Christians call Jesus the Lamb of God in worship and prayer; in some forms of the communion service the words 'Lamb of God' (the Agnus Dei) are sung or said before the bread and cup are shared.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the throne room: an emerald rainbow, a sea of glass, creatures who never stop singing. Your line was holy, holy, holy.

Someone is crying in the throne room. Not a creature. Not an elder. John. In the right hand of the one on the throne is a scroll, written inside and on the back, sealed with seven seals. A strong angel calls out: "Who is worthy to open the book, and to loose the seals thereof?" No one in heaven, on earth or under the earth can do it. And John writes, "I wept much, because no man was found worthy to open and to read the book." Then an elder leans over and tells him to stop crying, and look.

First, what John hears: "Weep not: behold, the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David, hath prevailed to open the book." The lion reaches back to Jacob's blessing, where Judah is called a lion's whelp. John is told to expect power. Second, what he sees: "and, lo, in the midst of the throne and of the four beasts, and in the midst of the elders, stood a Lamb as it had been slain." He hears lion. He sees lamb. Wounded, and still standing, at the center of yesterday's room. It has seven horns and seven eyes, the seven Spirits of God, but the text names the wound first. Third, the song. The creatures and elders fall down and sing a new song: "Thou art worthy to take the book, and to open the seals thereof: for thou wast slain." Not worthy in spite of being slain. Worthy because of it. Christians read the Lamb as Jesus, crucified and risen, the one John the Baptist pointed to, as you heard back in year two: "Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world." Fourth, why it matters. Revelation is full of beasts and dragons and armies. But the one at the center, the one who can open what no one else can, isn't the loudest or the fiercest. It's a lamb that was killed and stands anyway. In this book, that's what the lion looks like.
screen: `HE SEES: A LAMB, AS IT HAD BEEN SLAIN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a moment coming up where you'd usually push, an argument, a deadline, a person who tests you, and picture walking into it as a lamb would: steady and open-handed, not weak, with no fight to prove. Notice the strength that takes, and let your shoulders drop and your jaw loosen. If you pray, ask God for gentleness in it; if not, rehearse it gently in your mind.
The slain Lamb. Announced as a lion, seen as a lamb killed and still standing, and found worthy to open the scroll because it was slain.
Your line: the lamb is the lion. Wounded, and still standing at the center. Rest well.

1299.title: The four riders (Revelation 6)
1299.hook: conquest, war, famine and death ride out
1299.howItsDone: Christians pray for places suffering war and famine in their own prayers and in the prayers of the people during services, and some churches pray in lament using the Psalms' cry of 'how long'.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a lion announced and a lamb seen. Your line was the lamb is the lion.

The Lamb takes the scroll and breaks the first seal. One of the living creatures says, like thunder, "Come and see." A white horse comes out, its rider holding a bow, wearing a crown, going out "conquering, and to conquer." Second seal: a red horse, its rider given power "to take peace from the earth." Third: a black horse, its rider holding scales. Fourth: a pale horse, "and his name that sat on him was Death." Readers have named them conquest, war, famine and death. But a quieter moment in this chapter comes after the horses have gone.

First, the riders. The red one is given a great sword, "that they should kill one another." The black one carries scales, and a voice calls out prices: "A measure of wheat for a penny, and three measures of barley for a penny; and see thou hurt not the oil and the wine." Grain is dear, while the oil and the wine are spared. The pale one is Death, "and Hell followed with him." The white rider is argued over: plain conquest, or Christ, since a rider on a white horse returns later in the book. Second, who opens the seals: the Lamb. Readers differ on what that means. Some see judgment. Others see the world's own doings unveiled, with limits even on Death and Hell: power was given them "over the fourth part of the earth." Third, the fifth seal. Under the altar, John sees the souls of those killed for the word of God, crying: "How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?" It's the question of the Psalms: "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever?" Scripture lets people ask God that out loud, in heaven itself. Fourth, the answer isn't an explanation. "White robes were given unto every one of them; and it was said unto them, that they should rest yet for a little season." A robe, rest, and a question left open for now. If that cry is your own tonight, or you're thinking of harming yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

Bring one place of war or hunger to mind, just one, no flood of pictures, and hold it gently, the way you'd hold someone's hand in a hospital. If you pray, name that place before God, or borrow the words from under the altar, how long, O Lord; if not, keep it in your attention for a few slow breaths and let it matter to you.
The four riders. Conquest, war, famine and death, released as the Lamb opens the seals; then, from under the altar: how long?
Your line: how long? Even heaven makes room for that question, asked out loud. Until tomorrow.

1300.title: Every nation (Revelation 7:9–17)
1300.hook: a great multitude of every nation and tongue, and God wipes away every tear
1300.howItsDone: Revelation 7:9–17 is read at some Christian funerals and on All Saints' Day, as a picture of the saints from every nation gathered before God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the four riders, and a cry from under the altar. Your line was how long?

John hears a number first: "An hundred and forty and four thousand," sealed from the tribes of Israel, twelve thousand from each tribe, named one by one. A careful count. Then he looks, and what he sees can't be counted at all. Two days ago he heard lion and saw lamb, and some readers notice the same move here: a number heard, a crowd seen, too big for numbers. People from everywhere, standing before the throne in white, holding palm branches, all shouting at once.

First, the crowd, in the King James words: "a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands." Notice the list. The text doesn't melt them into one. In heaven, by this picture, languages are still languages. And they cry together: "Salvation to our God which sitteth upon the throne, and unto the Lamb." Second, who they are. An elder asks John: "What are these which are arrayed in white robes? and whence came they?" And John, who has seen so much already, says: "Sir, thou knowest." You tell me. The elder answers: "These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb." Robes made white by washing them in blood: Christians read it as the Lamb's death making people clean. Third, the care. After yesterday's famine: "They shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more; neither shall the sun light on them, nor any heat." The Lamb, the one who was slain, becomes their shepherd, and "shall lead them unto living fountains of waters." Fourth, the tears: "and God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes." It echoes Isaiah: "the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces." Wiping tears takes nearness; you have to be close enough to touch a face. Yesterday the question was how long. Today the answer isn't a date. It's a hand.

Let faces come, slowly, from everywhere you can think of, different skin, clothes and languages, nobody asked to stop being who they are: a neighbor, a coworker, someone you've argued with, people you'll never meet. If you pray, join the crowd's own words, "Salvation to our God which sitteth upon the throne, and unto the Lamb"; if not, just stand among them for a while, and breathe.
Every nation. John's great multitude that no one could number, from all nations, kindreds, peoples and tongues, fed and led by the Lamb, every tear wiped away.
Your line: every tear wiped. Not from across a room, but close enough to touch a face. Thirteen hundred days now.

1301.title: Silence in heaven (Revelation 8:1)
1301.hook: the seventh seal opens, and heaven goes silent for half an hour
1301.howItsDone: Some Christian services include a time of silence after the readings or before prayers, and some Christians keep times of silent prayer or retreat, drawing on verses like Psalm 46:10 and Habakkuk 2:20.

segments.voice: Yesterday, every nation: a crowd no one could count, and God wiping away every tear. Your line was every tear wiped.

Since the door opened in heaven, it has been loud. Lightning and thunder around the throne. Creatures that rest not day and night. A new song. Horses at the gallop. A cry from under the altar. A crowd from every nation shouting salvation. Then the Lamb opens the seventh seal, the last of the seven, and you'd expect the loudest moment of all. Instead, the whole book stops. One verse: "And when he had opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven about the space of half an hour."

First, the verse itself. It's short, and it doesn't explain. Even the length is loose: about half an hour. No song, no thunder, no voice is mentioned. Second, what the silence might mean. Some hear awe, the hush of the prophets: "But the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him." Others hear a held breath, a pause before the seven trumpets that come next. Revelation leaves both open. Third, what comes right after. Seven angels are given seven trumpets, and then another angel stands at the altar with a golden censer and much incense, "that he should offer it with the prayers of all saints upon the golden altar which was before the throne." And then: "the smoke of the incense, which came with the prayers of the saints, ascended up before God out of the angel's hand." Some readers suggest heaven goes quiet so the prayers can be heard, perhaps even the cry from under the altar, how long. The text doesn't say so. But after the quiet, the prayers rise. Fourth, the ordinary day. Heaven in this book is full of song, and it still has room for silence. A psalm puts it plainly: "Be still, and know that I am God." Some churches keep a silence after a reading or before the prayers. Some readers take from this that stillness belongs inside worship, not in the gaps around it.
screen: `INCENSE AND THE PRAYERS OF THE SAINTS.`

segments.voice: Heaven kept about half an hour; let these few minutes be the start of yours, with your phone face down and no words to fill the quiet, not even good ones. Let sounds come and go, a car, a fridge, your own breath, and let them pass like smoke rising. If you pray, let this be a prayer without words, rising like the incense; if not, just let the silence be what it is.
Silence in heaven. When the seventh seal opens, heaven goes quiet for about half an hour, and then the prayers of the saints rise like incense.
Your line: silence in heaven. Even a heaven full of song keeps room for quiet. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1302.title: The little scroll (Revelation 10)
1302.hook: sweet as honey in the mouth, bitter in the stomach
1302.howItsDone: Christians who read Revelation 10 alongside Ezekiel 2–3 often hear it as a picture of receiving God's word: preachers and readers speak of taking scripture in slowly, letting it become part of them, sweet and demanding at once.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seventh seal opened and heaven went quiet for about half an hour. Your line was silence in heaven.

An angel comes down wrapped in a cloud, a rainbow over his head. He plants his right foot on the sea and his left on the land, and cries out like a lion roaring. Seven thunders answer. John reaches to write down what they said, and a voice stops him: seal it up, and don't write it. So there are words in Revelation that Revelation keeps to itself. Then a stranger order: go and take the little book open in the angel's hand. John asks for it. The angel hands it over and says: eat it. That little book is today's word.
screen: `ONE FOOT ON THE SEA, ONE ON THE LAND.`

segments.voice: The King James calls it a little book; the title here says little scroll. Either way, words small enough to hold in one hand. First, the warning comes before the meal: "it shall make thy belly bitter, but it shall be in thy mouth sweet as honey." John eats it anyway, and it's exactly as promised: "it was in my mouth sweet as honey: and as soon as I had eaten it, my belly was bitter." Second, John isn't alone. Ezekiel was handed a scroll written with "lamentations, and mourning, and woe." He ate it too: "it was in my mouth as honey for sweetness." A scroll full of grief, and it tasted like honey. John's story leans on his. Third, why bitter? The text doesn't say outright, so readers differ. Some hear the calling: God's word is sweet to receive and heavy to carry, because the very next line is an order: "Thou must prophesy again before many peoples, and nations, and tongues, and kings." Others hear the message itself: God's victory, and suffering still on the way, in one mouthful. Fourth, this isn't only a vision. Plenty of true things land this way. A diagnosis that finally explains the pain. An honest word from a friend. A calling you know is yours, and know will cost you. Sweet to hear, and then it has to go all the way down.

Let one truth come to mind that's good to know and hard to carry, about your life, your family or your work. Don't fix it; hold it the way John held the little book, noticing where the sweet part is and where the hard part sits in your body. If you pray, bring both to God at once; if not, let both be true together for a minute.
The little scroll. The book John was told to eat in Revelation ten: sweet as honey in his mouth, bitter once it was inside him.
Your line: sweet and bitter. From a knock at the door in Laodicea, through a Lamb, four riders and silence, this week ran to a book you eat. See you tomorrow.
